US Senate GOP leader Thune reelected for next 2 years even after election losses
U.S. Senate Republican Leader John Thune, of South Dakota, speaks to reporters during a press conference in the Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)
WASHINGTON — South Dakota Sen. John Thune will remain Republican leader next Congress despite the GOP’s loss of the chamber’s majority in this year’s midterm elections.
GOP senators voted behind closed doors Tuesday to keep Thune at the helm and reelected Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso as their whip. Neither was challenged.
The other members of Senate Republican leadership will include Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton of Arkansas, Republican Policy Committee Chair Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, Vice Chair of the Republican Conference James Lankford of Oklahoma and National Republican Senatorial Committee Chair Bernie Moreno of Ohio.
‘Listening intently’
Thune said after the meeting that he and other Republicans were not happy with the results of the midterm elections but will focus more on voters’ concerns in the years ahead.
“As we move forward, we are going to be listening intently to what the American people are saying,” he said. “And I think right now the issue that matters the most to them, like I said, is the cost of living.”
Thune pledged to extend the lame duck session that spans November and December to give Republicans more time to confirm nominees and approve legislation before handing over power to Democrats in early January. Republicans now hold 53 seats and The Associated Press projects they will have 44 next year, with results in Alaska and Mississippi still not called.
“Our conference is committed to being here to do whatever it takes to get as much done as we can,” he said. “That means extending the calendar here, the number of days we’re here, the number of hours we’re here, the number of votes we may end up taking. But we are going to finish this legislative session strong.”
Push for nominations
There was an attempt by several Republican senators to delay decisions about leadership for at least a week, but they were ultimately unsuccessful.
Missouri Sen. Eric Schmitt said after the meeting that Republican leaders had committed to clear as many nominees through the chamber as possible. Democrats are unlikely to approve President Donald Trump’s picks for the federal bench or administration roles after January.
“We’re definitely going to maximize the next 54 days for sure,” he said.
Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley said ahead of the vote that he wanted to delay until later this year to give Republicans an opportunity to “change course” following the election results.
“It’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here,” he said, questioning why Republican leaders didn’t put bills on the floor to lower the cost of gasoline and healthcare.
“If you don’t put people first, sooner or later people turn on you,” Hawley said. “And I think that this party thought we can just do whatever we want. People voted for us in ’24, we’ll do whatever we want. No you can’t. You’ve got to do stuff that actually helps people.”
‘Never disappoint voters again’
Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson said following a morning conference meeting that Republicans were “voicing opinions on all sides of the issues.”
“It’s one of those times in the Republican Conference, you kind of go, ‘We got … some smart people, and we’re having a very good respectful conversation,’” Johnson said.
Ohio’s Moreno said later in the day that Republicans are committed to “never disappoint voters again.”
“We’re firmly aware of the consequences now, and that’s the strategy we’re going to employ in 2028,” he said.
60 votes needed
Thune will still have considerable power as minority leader as long as Democrats keep a rule that requires 60 senators vote to advance legislation.
The hurdle forces bipartisanship on major proposals. But even if Democrats were to remove it next Congress, bills would still need Trump’s support to become law, unless there are supermajorities in each chamber to override a veto.

Senate Republicans Choose Thune to Lead in Minority
Senate Republicans opted for continuity on Tuesday, keeping John Thune in charge as their conference heads into the minority next year. The South Dakota senator was reelected by acclamation in a closed-door meeting after conservatives failed in a push to delay the leadership vote in the hopes another candidate would emerge, Politico reports. Sen. Rick Scott of Florida said he wanted to know the plan for the months ahead, reports the Hill. "We have 55 days until the Democrats take over," he said, "so I want to know what we're going to do between now and then to get stuff done."
The Senate majority leader, who was running unopposed, was widely expected to prevail in the secret ballot, but senators including Sen. Jim Justice of West Virginia expressed misgivings during meetings Tuesday, noting that the party lost at least seven seats in the midterms, the AP reports. There is a "legitimate argument that, good gracious, if we lost as badly as we lost, why would we continue on with the same leadership?" he said, though he added that GOP leadership "didn't cause this problem to happen."
Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, who had backed the delay, said Thune delivered a "heartfelt" address and argued he had been unfairly targeted by some in the party's base. Before the vote, he noted there was nobody else on the ballot and said, "that's part of our problem, who would want the job?" In a statement, Thune said he "appreciated the opportunity to have an open, honest, and transparent conversation with my colleagues" and he is "honored to have their continued trust and support to lead the Senate Republican Conference in the 120th Congress."

sources.news_title: Thune will lead Republicans through the minority
sources.text:
Thune will lead Republicans through the minority
South Dakotan wins reelection as GOP leader, despite a push from some senators to delay
Senate Majority Leader John Thune was reelected as the Republican leader on Tuesday and will steer the conference through their time in the minority.
The South Dakotan ran uncontested despite a push from some of his colleagues to delay the leadership elections following Republicans’ stunning defeats last week in the midterms, which saw them lose at least seven seats and the majority.
“Obviously, the election result was not what we hoped for,” Thune told reporters, referring to the midterms. “But I think it’s important that we take the lessons from that and internalize the message the American people were sending to us.”
While he and the rest of the leadership slate sailed through the conference contests by voice vote, it wasn’t without drama.
Before the leadership elections began in the Old Supreme Court Chamber early Tuesday morning, the conference held a meeting at the request of a group of GOP five senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis.
The conversation, which several senators described as “frank,” ended up pushing back the leadership elections by a few hours. But they were not postponed to another day as some had hoped.
“This has never been anything against John Thune,” said Johnson, as he made good on his commitment to leave the room early if the conference proceeded with its election. “What I didn’t agree with was holding the election right away, giving nobody an opportunity to really challenge any leadership position.”
“Part of the issue here is who wants the job? God bless him for serving,” Johnson added.
The conference conversation Tuesday morning turned into an “open-mic” with both conservatives and those who lost their elections speaking, according to senators.
Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., told reporters, “To rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”
But no contender to Thune emerged despite the angst, and a motion to proceed to the election, introduced by Thune’s fellow South Dakotan Sen. Mike Rounds, was accepted.
Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters who rejected Republicans last week were reacting to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living, not to how Senate leaders were running the conference.
“I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem,” Paul said.
Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., was reelected to his position, as was the chairman of the Senate Republican Conference, Tom Cotton of Arkansas. Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma was again selected as vice chair of the conference, while Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia was reelected as Republican Policy Committee chair.
“Our first step is to make sure the American people know that we heard what they said, and the American people’s priorities are our priorities. That’s the way we regain their trust,” Barrasso said afterward.
Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio got the nod to chair the National Republican Senatorial Committee, meaning he will helm the campaign arm as the party looks ahead to the uncertain waters of 2028.
Moreno said, “I was in the retail automobile business, so when you don’t listen to your customers, your customers punish you. I think we have to own it, and I think we have to learn from it.”
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., said on Monday evening, “What we as a conference right now need is honesty. We need focus. We need to try to reach a consensus on what we need to change.”
Kennedy was among those pushing to delay the leadership elections and told reporters on Tuesday he voted present instead of yes on whether to proceed to them.
Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., who ran for GOP leader twice — once in 2022 against Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., and in 2024 against Thune — declined to run again to challenge Thune. But in a Dear Colleague letter on Monday, he detailed what he’d like to see in the lame-duck session before Democrats take power, including confirming every nominee President Donald Trump has sent to the Senate, funding the government without an omnibus, banning stock trading, passing the permitting bill that is advancing this week in the Senate, passing the National Defense Authorization Act, balancing the budget and pushing through a sweeping voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act.
Senate Republicans on Tuesday also voted on a resolution on their path forward that was spurred by a motion from Scott, aides said.
“It is the sense of the GOP Conference that we will maximize the 54 days we have with congressional majorities, to confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of, to pass our core Republican priorities, and to do everything humanly possible to pass a reconciliation bill before Jan. 3,” the resolution reads in part.
That long list of goals highlights the expectations Thune has faced as leader, where he led one-third of Republicans’ trifecta in Washington. In the next Congress, Democrats will hold the majority in both chambers of Congress after their larger-than-expected wins, while Trump finishes out his term as president.
Thune said he told his conference: “As I look back on the last couple of years, my question is, what would you have me do differently?”
“Given the constraints we had to deal with, all the stuff that was coming at us on a daily basis, a narrow margin in the House, the White House, the Democrats over here who were obstructing two long government shutdowns — I think we came out of it as well as could have been expected, and got a lot of stuff done,” Thune told reporters.
“If you believe the exit polls, it was the war, it was the economy, it was inflation, it was fuel prices,” Thune added. “So no, I wasn’t apologizing for anything that we did. And I think on the political side, I don’t know what else I could have done.”

sources.news_title: ‘Ultimate betrayal’: MAGA erupts after Senate Republicans stick with Thune
sources.text:
Senate Republicans sparked outrage among some of President Donald Trump’s MAGA supporters Tuesday after voting behind closed doors to reelect Sen. John Thune (R-SD) as their leader despite the party’s midterm election losses.
Thune, who ran unopposed, will become Senate minority leader when Democrats take control in January, according to media reports.
“I am honored to have their continued trust and support to lead the 120th Congress,” Thune wrote in a celebratory post shortly after the vote.
But not everybody in the party was happy about Thune's return as GOP Senate leader.
“GOP Senators have once again stabbed voters in the back by supporting John Thune for re-election as minority leader behind closed doors,” far-right social media personality Bad Hombre wrote on X.
“This is completely unacceptable,” he added, announcing that he was leaving the Republican Party after 14 years.
Another self-described three-time Trump voter called the decision “the ultimate betrayal.”
MAGA podcaster Benny Johnson also weighed in.
“Senate Republicans just held a closed-door vote to re-elect John Thune as Senate minority leader for the upcoming Congress,” he wrote. “Unbelievable…”
The backlash followed an unsuccessful effort by several Republican senators to postpone the leadership elections.
Sen. Ron Johnson (R-WI), who walked out rather than participate in the vote, told reporters, “I really don’t like walking out but that’s what I said I would do and I did it,” according to reporting by Semafor’s Burgess Everett.
Despite his protest, Johnson said Thune had been “unfairly attacked by our base.”
Meanwhile, House Republicans elected Jim Jordan (R-OH) to become their next minority leader.

sources.news_title: John Thune retains Senate GOP leadership after midterm losses
sources.text:
WASHINGTON — Senate Republicans reelected Sen. John Thune of South Dakota as their leader on Tuesday, retaining the bulk of their current leadership team one week after midterm losses that cost the party control of the Senate.
Thune, who has served as majority leader since early 2025 after succeeding longtime leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, won by acclamation in a closed-door conference meeting in the Old Senate Chamber. No senator challenged him. The rest of the top leadership team was also reelected: Sen. John Barrasso of Wyoming as whip, Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas as conference chair, Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia as policy committee chair, and Sen. James Lankford of Oklahoma as conference vice chair.
Sen. Bernie Moreno of Ohio is set to take over as chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, the party’s Senate campaign arm, succeeding Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina.
The vote followed hours of sometimes tense discussions about last week’s election results, in which Republicans lost at least seven Senate seats and lost control of both chambers of Congress. A group of conservative senators, led by Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, had pushed to delay the leadership elections for further discussion of the losses and the party’s path forward. That effort failed, and Johnson left the room as voting began. Sens. Rick Scott of Florida, Mike Lee of Utah, and others had joined calls for more time.
“I appreciated the opportunity to have an open, honest, and transparent conversation with my colleagues today, and I am honored to have their continued trust and support to lead the Senate Republican Conference in the 120th Congress,” Thune said in a statement after the vote.
Critics argued the scale of the losses demanded a deeper reckoning before locking in leaders.
“If you don’t think after losing seven Senate seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri told reporters. Johnson and others had sought a clearer plan for the remaining weeks of the current Congress, including possible action on defense spending and other priorities, before Democrats take control in January.
Supporters of the current team pointed to Thune’s relationships across the conference and the absence of a viable alternative. Lankford described “widespread support” for Thune, noting his practice of hearing out different viewpoints. President Donald Trump stayed on the sidelines; he has previously called Thune a “very fine man” while saying the choice belonged to the senators.
Thune will continue as majority leader through the end of the current Congress before becoming minority leader when the new Congress convenes. The elections came exactly one week after Election Day, as Senate Republicans begin preparing for life in the minority and assessing the results ahead of the 2028 cycle.

By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
WASHINGTON — Senate Republicans reelected Sen. John Thune of South Dakota as their leader Tuesday, Nov. 10, despite objections from conservative lawmakers who demanded a change in direction following the party’s sweeping midterm election losses. Thune ran unopposed in the closed-door, secret-ballot election and will become Senate minority leader when Democrats assume control of the chamber in January.
The decision followed three contentious Republican conference meetings in which senators debated whether to proceed with the leadership election or postpone it to allow more time to examine the party’s political setbacks. According to The Associated Press, the conference ultimately voted to move forward despite opposition from several conservatives who argued that maintaining the existing leadership without a broader review would send the wrong message to voters.
Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who led the effort to delay the election, walked out of the meeting as voting began. Johnson had circulated a letter urging Republican senators to reconsider the timing of the leadership contest and evaluate what went wrong in the Nov. 3 elections, when Republicans lost at least seven Senate seats and surrendered their majority. Two additional contests in Alaska and Mississippi remained uncalled Tuesday, leaving the final composition of the incoming Senate uncertain.
“We need to have some real soul-searching,” Johnson said ahead of the election. “We can’t just continue on business as usual — that kind of defeat demands change.”
Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., also questioned the decision to retain the party’s leadership without first addressing the election results. Hawley argued that Republican senators needed more time to discuss their priorities and consider whether alternative candidates might emerge if the election were postponed.
“I just think that we’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think that to just rush into this and just ratify all of the same leadership, what message does that send?” Hawley told reporters. “If you don’t think after losing seven Senate seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on.”
The leadership dispute extended beyond Thune’s reelection. Several conservatives pressed Republican leaders to establish a legislative strategy for the remaining weeks of the 119th Congress, arguing that the party should use its final opportunity to advance President Donald Trump’s priorities before Democrats take control Jan. 3, 2027. The proposed agenda includes additional administration confirmations, government funding legislation, defense spending and measures addressing domestic energy production.
“We need a plan to get the Republican agenda done,” Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., said during the discussions.
Other Republican senators defended Thune, arguing that the election losses reflected broader political circumstances rather than failures by the Senate leadership team. Sen. Jim Justice, R-W.Va., acknowledged the arguments for reconsidering the party’s direction but said the current leadership had performed its responsibilities effectively.
Justice said there was a “legitimate argument that, good gracious, if we lost as badly as we lost, why would we continue on with the same leadership?” However, he added that the leadership team “didn’t cause this problem to happen” and said its members had done a good job.
Sen. Jim Lankford, R-Okla., also defended Thune, citing his relationships with Republican senators and willingness to consider differing opinions before making decisions. Thune succeeded Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., as Republican leader in January 2025, promising a more collaborative approach to managing the conference after McConnell’s lengthy tenure.
Thune’s leadership has nevertheless drawn criticism from some conservative Republicans over his handling of legislation supported by Trump, particularly efforts to change Senate procedural rules. Although Thune has generally supported the president’s agenda, he has resisted calls to eliminate the legislative filibuster to advance voting legislation requiring proof of citizenship.
The disagreement has frustrated Trump and some of his supporters, who argue that Republicans should use their congressional majorities to enact priorities without allowing procedural obstacles to prevent final votes. Thune has maintained that preserving the filibuster protects the Senate’s institutional role and could prevent Democrats from advancing legislation by simple majority when Republicans are in the minority.
Trump has publicly expressed support for Thune despite those differences. The president hosted the senator and his family at the White House in October and described him Monday as “a very fine man,” while saying the leadership decision belonged to Republican senators.
The leadership debate reported by Roll Call also reflected disagreements over the causes of Republican losses. Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., identified the cost of living, high gasoline prices and the war involving Iran as important factors in the election results, arguing that voters’ dissatisfaction should not automatically be attributed to Thune.
“The cost of living defeated us,” Paul said. “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem.”
Republicans now face a limited legislative window before their majority expires. Lawmakers are considering government funding measures and an energy permitting proposal that advanced with bipartisan support Monday. The party also intends to confirm additional Trump administration nominees before Democrats gain control of the Senate’s legislative agenda and confirmation process.
Thune acknowledged the election setbacks in a Senate floor speech Monday, describing the results as a “tough night” for Republicans. He said the party would remain willing to cooperate with Democrats on certain issues while opposing proposals that conflict with Republican priorities.
The November elections have also created leadership questions for Democrats, with Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer facing calls from some progressive organizations and labor groups to step aside despite his party’s victories. The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers, which represents approximately 600,000 members, urged Schumer on Monday to make way for a new generation of Democratic leadership.
For Republicans, Thune’s reelection resolves the immediate leadership question but leaves broader disagreements over political strategy and legislative priorities unsettled. The conference must now determine how to use its remaining weeks in the majority while preparing to confront a Democratic-controlled Congress during the final two years of Trump’s presidency.
Thune will remain Senate majority leader through the conclusion of the current Congress before assuming the minority leadership position in January, placing him at the center of Republican efforts to challenge Democratic legislation, negotiate with the incoming majority and defend the administration’s agenda.

sources.news_title: Senate Republicans vote to keep John Thune as leader after steep election losses
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Republicans reelected South Dakota Sen. John Thune as their leader Tuesday after a tense day of private discussions about steep losses in the midterm elections that cost them their majority.
Thune was always expected to prevail, as he is popular with his GOP colleagues and was running unopposed in the secret-ballot election. But Senate Republicans vented their frustrations in three separate meetings Tuesday after an election wipeout that cost them at least seven Senate seats.
Some Republicans had tried to delay the leadership decision, but the conference voted 31-15 to proceed with a vote after Thune made his case to his colleagues, laying out his vision for the minority and also promising that they will try and do as much as they can in their final two months in the majority.
“We're going to make the most of the time we've got,” Thune said after he was elected by acclamation, without a roll call vote.
As for next year, Thune said that told his colleagues that they will "come out swinging, and realize we've got a lot of work to be done to get back in the majority.”
The day's meetings were a combination of venting and thoughtful conversation, with some senators who won and lost elections this year sharing their thoughts and others questioning if they should be quickly endorsing their leadership slate after a significant defeat.
West Virginia Sen. Jim Justice said that there was a “legitimate argument that, good gracious, if we lost as badly as we lost, why would we continue on with the same leadership?”
At the same time, the current GOP leadership “didn’t cause this problem to happen,” Justice said. “They do a good job.”
Republicans' angst and indecision come as frustrated Republicans are just beginning to reckon with what the election results mean for their future — and for their relationship with President Donald Trump, as voters resoundingly rejected their two years of single-party rule in Congress and the White House. Two additional Senate races remain uncalled in Alaska and Mississippi that could further deplete their numbers.
“If you don’t think after losing seven Senate seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” said Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley, who voted to delay the elections. He said he wasn’t aware of anyone else running for leader, but “maybe there would be” if they waited.
No alternative to Thune emerged
Thune, who replaced Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky as leader in early 2025, pushed back on the idea of a delay, questioning what it would achieve. Several senators backed him up, including his South Dakota colleague Mike Rounds, who countered the calls for postponement with the successful motion to vote immediately.
Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, who was reelected to her leadership position as GOP policy chair, said that Thune wasn't the reason they suffered losses. “I don't think it was the fault of our leadership, quite frankly," she said.
Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., said he had confidence in the newly re-elected slate. The discussion was mainly "about policy,” he said.
Republicans in the meeting were also pushing Thune to stay in session around the clock in the coming weeks to push through war spending and other party priorities before they lose power in January. Republicans are trying to wrap up the year’s work — funding the government, confirming Trump's nominees and seeing if there are some issues where they can work with Democrats, including an energy permitting bill that moved forward on a bipartisan vote Monday evening.
Before the vote on Thune, the conference adopted a resolution to maximize the time they have left and to “confirm every judicial nominee and every executive nominee that the conference approves of.”
“We need a plan to get the Republican agenda done,” said Florida Sen. Rick Scott.
Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson circulated a letter before the meeting asking for the delay. He said the conference needs to do some “real soul-searching” but also conceded that there was no one else on the ballot.
“That's part of our problem, who would want the job?” he said on Monday, turning to a reporter and joking, “Do you want it?”
Oklahoma Sen. Jim Lankford said that there was “widespread support” among Republican senators for Thune, who has made it a point to hear out different viewpoints before he makes major decisions and has maintained close relationships with the rank and file — a different approach from his predecessor, McConnell.
Lankford said he supported having the elections on Tuesday because many of the new GOP senators were already in town for freshman orientation.
“It’s a pretty complicated role to be able to manage,” Lankford said of Thune's leadership post. “No one wants that job.”
Thune has navigated Trump in his first two years as leader
Thune has spent much of the last two years navigating Trump, who has often been at odds with the Senate.
While backing Trump on most policies, Thune has refused to change Senate rules and scrap the filibuster to pass voting legislation that would require proof of citizenship for all voters — a position that frustrated Trump and enraged some in the president's political base.
Still, Trump hosted Thune and his family at the White House in October. He said Monday that the GOP leader is “a very fine man.” The election is “up to the Senate,” Trump said.
Thune has emphasized his collaborative approach to his colleagues and pointed out what they did get done in the last two years — including Trump's sweeping tax and spending cuts legislation and an attempt at reining in the chaotic annual spending process.
“We're not going to be running this place next year, the Democrats are,” Thune said afterward. “But you can be assured that we will be very, very active in asserting conservative priorities.”

sources.news_title: Senate Republicans voting on whether to keep Thune as leader
sources.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Senate Republicans reelected South Dakota Sen. John Thune as their leader Tuesday after a tense day of private discussions about steep losses in the midterm elections that cost them their majority.
Thune was always expected to prevail, as he is popular with his GOP colleagues and was running unopposed in the secret-ballot election. But Senate Republicans vented their frustrations in three separate meetings Tuesday after an election wipeout that cost them at least seven Senate seats.
Some Republicans had tried to delay the leadership decision, but the conference voted 31-15 to proceed. Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson led the effort to postpone and walked out when it failed. The closed-door meetings were held in the small Old Senate Chamber with few aides in attendance.
As the conference debated earlier in the day, West Virginia Sen. Jim Justice said “we want to be thoughtful and do the right thing.”
He said there was a “legitimate argument that, good gracious, if we lost as badly as we lost, why would we continue on with the same leadership?”
At the same time, the current GOP leadership “didn’t cause this problem to happen,” Justice said. “They do a good job.”
Republicans' angst and indecision come as frustrated Republicans are just beginning to reckon with what the election results mean for their future — and for their relationship with President Donald Trump, as voters resoundingly rejected their two years of single-party rule in Congress and the White House. Two additional Senate races remain uncalled in Alaska and Mississippi that could further deplete their numbers.
“I just think that we’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think that to just rush into this and just ratify all of the same leadership, what message does that send?” Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley told reporters after the first meeting.
“If you don’t think after losing seven Senate seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” said Hawley, who voted to delay the elections. He said he wasn't aware of anyone else running for leader, but “maybe there would be” if they waited.
Others said Thune wasn't the problem. “I don't think it was the fault of our leadership, quite frankly," said West Virginia Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, who was reelected to her leadership position as GOP policy chair.
Thune, who replaced Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky as leader in early 2025, said before the meeting that they would have a “very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”
No alternative to Thune emerged
Hawley said the discussion was a “frank” and “honest” open microphone meeting and some senators discussed their own races this year — some who won, and some who lost.
Republicans in the meeting were also pushing Thune to stay in session around the clock in the coming weeks to push through war spending and other party priorities before they lose power in January.
“We need a plan to get the Republican agenda done,” said Florida Sen. Rick Scott.
Before the meeting, Johnson, the Wisconsin senator, had circulated a letter asking for the delay. He said the conference needs to do some “real soul-searching” but also conceded that there was no one else on the ballot.
“That's part of our problem, who would want the job?” he said, turning to a reporter and joking, “Do you want it?”
Oklahoma Sen. Jim Lankford said that there was “widespread support” among Republican senators for Thune, who has made it a point to hear out different viewpoints before he makes major decisions and has maintained close relationships with the rank and file — a different approach from his predecessor, McConnell.
Lankford said he supported having the elections on Tuesday because many of the new GOP senators were already in town for freshman orientation.
“It’s a pretty complicated role to be able to manage,” Lankford said of Thune's leadership post. “No one wants that job.”
Walking into the meeting, South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds said most senators were ready to move forward. It is time to have “leadership in place,” he said.
Thune has navigated Trump in his first two years as leader
Thune has spent much of the last two years navigating Trump, who has often been at odds with the Senate.
While backing Trump on most policies, Thune has refused to change Senate rules and scrap the filibuster to pass voting legislation that would require proof of citizenship for all voters — a position that frustrated Trump and enraged some in the president's political base.
Still, Trump hosted Thune and his family at the White House in October. He said Monday that the GOP leader is “a very fine man.” The election is “up to the Senate,” Trump said.
The soul-searching comes as lawmakers are trying to wrap up the year’s work — funding the government and seeing if there are some issues where they can work together, including an energy permitting bill that moved forward on a bipartisan vote Monday evening.
Thune has emphasized his collaborative approach to his colleagues and pointed out what they did get done in the last year — including Trump's sweeping tax and spending cuts legislation and an attempt at reining in the chaotic annual spending process.
In a Senate floor speech Monday, his first extended remarks since the election, Thune said the midterm election was a “tough night” and previewed his pitch to his colleagues who may be looking for answers on how they will navigate the minority.
Republicans will be willing to work with Democrats, Thune said, but “the American people are not looking for socialist government and leftist fantasies.”
Associated Press reporter Seung Min Kim contributed to this report.

Well, so much for the guy whose name is on the blame line taking the heat for a disaster.
Yes, you guessed it; Senate Republicans have confirmed Sen. John Thune (R-SD) to be Senate Minority Leader for the 120th Congress. Yes, really.
There was neither an exodus nor a mass housecleaning in the Senate GOP leadership, despite frustration and rumblings of discontent among some lawmakers reeling from last week’s devastating midterm losses.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., secured another term as the top Republican behind the closed doors of the Old Senate Chamber, where lawmakers charted their course for their few remaining weeks in power and beyond.
His victory comes after a cohort of Republicans led by Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., demanded that the Senate GOP pause its scheduled leadership elections to debrief on their stunning midterm losses.
After taking the roundhouse punch that the Republican Party took last week, one would think a shakeup would be in order. But, we voted for them, and they voted for John Thune. There weren't many others who wanted the job, and granted, there are some difficult times ahead for Senate Republicans; barring some disaster, the map doesn't favor the GOP retaking the Senate until, perhaps, 2030 or even 2032.
But, it seems, there was no alternative. So, back to the same old well.
The night before, Thune was adamant that he’d still run but was unsure of the outcome.
"That's the hope," Thune said when asked if he had the Senate GOP’s support. "You never know right until they vote."
Before the vote, Johnson and a handful of others believed there should be a shakeup in leadership, but didn’t offer an alternative to Thune.
"After the stunning defeat, you just can't continue on business as usual," Johnson said. "I mean, that kind of defeat demands change."
This will probably cause some discomfiture, not only with Senate Republicans, but with Republican Party members who are understandably frustrated with the shellacking the party took in last week's midterms. We should bear in mind, of course, that this isn't the first time this has happened; midterm shakeups have happened as far back as President Truman's first midterm election in 1946, when Senate Democrats lost 12 Senate seats to Republicans. And many of us remember the beating President Clinton's Democrats took in 1994 when Democrats lost eight Senate seats to the Republicans, and then in 2010, when President Obama's Democrats lost six Senate seats to the GOP.
Still, the 2026 midterms are looking to cost the Senate Republicans seven to nine seats, and while that's not a record, it sure isn't good.
So, for now, it's Minority Leader Thune, and we'll see how well he does. Success is the best redemption, and if he can manage to herd this now-admittedly smaller herd of cats to a few wins — or even just hold off disaster — he may end up framing well as the top man in the new minority.
Even so, for now, there will be a lot of Republicans that will look on this with displeasure, and Sen. sources.text:
Congress live updates as GOP picks House and Senate leaders, Hegseth impeachment vote is killed
What to know about Congress today:
- House and Senate Republicans held internal elections for their leadership teams on Tuesday as they prepare to become the minority in January, with lawmakers in each chamber taking different approaches to their upcoming stint in the proverbial wilderness.
- In the House, hard-line conservative Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio defeated Majority Leader Steve Scalise to become minority leader. Jordan is a top ally of President Trump and the current chairman of the House Judiciary Committee who has battled with Democrats for years.
- Across the Capitol, Senate Republicans retained their top leadership, unanimously electing Sen. John Thune of South Dakota as minority leader. Some GOP senators had called for a delay in the final vote to discuss the results of the midterm elections, but Thune ultimately emerged unscathed.
- The House blocked an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his handling of the war with Iran and other issues. Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who led the push, was the only Republican to vote against a motion to send the impeachment bid to a committee, effectively tabling it. Hegseth decried the effort as a "political spectacle."
House blocks effort to impeach Hegseth
The House has blocked an effort led by GOP Rep. Thomas Massie to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, largely over the war with Iran.
The House voted 211 to 204 to refer the resolution to the House Judiciary Committee, effectively killing it. Massie was the lone Republican to vote with all Democrats against it.
House holding initial vote on Hegseth impeachment
The House has begun voting on whether to block the impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
If it passes, the resolution will be referred to a committee, effectively killing it. If it passes, the House could move forward with votes to impeach Hegseth as soon as Wednesday.
Thune says Republicans will "finish this legislative session strong"
Senate Majority Leader John Thune, speaking after he was reelected as GOP leader, outlined a plan to "finish this legislative session strong," emphasizing the need to move judicial and executive branch nominees, fund the government and "make the most of the time that we've got."
Thune said the conference is committed to staying in Washington, extending the calendar and the number of work days to finish out their work.
Jordan gives brief statement after winning election as minority leader
Rep. Jim Jordan spoke briefly after winning the leadership election.
"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. When Democrats offer more government, we'll offer more freedom. And we will bring that fight in committee, on the floor and on the stump every single day," he said, before thanking his colleagues for their support.
He did not take any questions.
Mike Johnson: "Easier to keep a group together when you're in the minority"
House Speaker Mike Johnson praised incoming Minority Leader Jim Jordan as a mentor of his when he was first elected to Congress.
"He's always been regarded as a leader by the conference, and he's going to do an extraordinary job," Johnson said after leadership elections.
Johnson said he talked with Jordan earlier Tuesday about keeping the often-divided conference united.
"It is easier to keep a group together when you're in the minority," he said.
Johnson would not reveal who he voted for, calling Jordan and Majority Leader Steve Scalise "both my brothers."
Schumer says he's "confident" he'll be elected majority leader
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told reporters he is "confident" he'll be elected majority leader when Democrats take control.
"I'm confident I will be elected majority leader," Schumer said during a press conference at the Capitol.
Schumer has been the top Senate Democrat for nearly 10 years.
Ernst says she had a "productive" meeting with Turek
Outgoing Republican Sen. Joni Ernst of Iowa posted a photo with Democratic Sen.-elect Josh Turek of Iowa, saying they had a "productive" conversation. Turek won Ernst's seat in last week's election. Ernst decided not to run for reelection, and Turek beat Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson for the seat.
"Welcomed Senator-elect Josh Turek to the Capitol today!" Ernst wrote. "We had a productive conversation about the responsibilities and honor of serving in the US Senate and representing the great people of Iowa. We will work together to ensure the voices of all Iowans are heard and their needs continue to be met during the transition."
Senate Republicans reelect Thune without opposition
Senate Republicans elected John Thune as leader by acclamation, his spokesperson said, meaning there were no dissenters.
Senate Republicans also reelected Sen. John Barrasso as whip, Sen. Tom Cotton as conference chair and Sen. Shelley Moore Capito as policy chair.
Senate GOP proceeding to leadership elections, Johnson says
Sen. Ron Johnson, emerging from the Senate GOP conference meeting, said Republicans accepted a motion to proceed to leadership elections, which are now underway.
Johnson had pushed to delay the elections to discuss the path forward after the midterm elections. Republicans met behind closed doors for two hours earlier Tuesday, before reconvening in the afternoon.
Sanders says he won't back Schumer as Democratic leader
Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont said at a press conference at the Capitol that he will not support Sen. Chuck Schumer for majority leader, becoming the most prominent progressive to oppose Schumer's candidacy to date.
"I personally have known Chuck Schumer for over 30 years, and I like Chuck. Nobody who works harder than Chuck Schumer," Sanders said. "But in my view, the time is now for change, and I will not be supporting Chuck to be reelected as the Democratic leader."
Sanders was alongside Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a Michigan Democrat. Slotkin said she is "not actively seeking this job," but seeking change.
Asked about possible challengers to Schumer, Sanders cited Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland. Van Hollen told reporters this week that he wasn't closing the door on the option.
Democrats are expected to vote for their leaders next month.
House Democratic leaders aren't whipping votes for Hegseth impeachment vote
House Democratic leaders aren't whipping votes to impeach Hegseth, said Rep. Pete Aguilar, chair of the House Democratic Caucus. That means that Democratic leaders aren't pushing their members to vote to impeach, letting them decide for their districts.
"It's not being whipped," Aguilar told reporters. "Members are going to have to make their own decisions based on the articles of impeachment. We didn't put our finger on the scale."
Aguilar said he'll vote yes on impeaching Hegseth, as will House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries. But members will make their own decisions, Aguilar said, "and we respect that."
Emmer wins election as GOP whip, Jordan's No. 2
Rep. Tom Emmer of Minnesota won election to remain as the House GOP's whip, the position he currently holds. The role is the second highest-ranking in the minority, meaning Emmer will be Jordan's No. 2.
Emmer defeated a challenge from Rep. August Pfluger of Texas for the job.
Jim Jordan wins election as House minority leader
Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio has won election as the House GOP's leader in the next Congress, defeating current Majority Leader Steve Scalise. The vote was 106 to 73, sources familiar with the tally told CBS News.
Jordan is a hard-line conservative and close ally of President Trump. His ascension to minority leader represents a significant shakeup for House Republicans, who are looking to rebuild after losing more than 40 House seats.
Senate Republicans reconvene ahead of expected vote on delaying leadership election
Senate Republicans are reconvening, after they recessed following a two-hour meeting Tuesday morning. They're expected to vote on whether to delay the leadership elections. If that effort falls short, senators will move on to conducting the leadership elections themselves.
Asked about his pitch to Republicans ahead of the meeting, Thune told CBS News, "I'm kind of hearing everybody out, and then I'll summarize what I heard."
Mississippi's Hyde-Smith says she "had a very good campaign" as race remains up in the air
Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi, who's still locked in a race against Democrat Scott Colom that remains up in the air, told reporters that "we've got a lot of votes still out, and we're counting, and we hope to come back and represent them the way that we have."
Colom is leading Hyde-Smith, the GOP incumbent, by more than 2,500 votes as of Tuesday.
"People vote with their wallets, and gas prices are high," Hyde-Smith said of the dynamics in the race.
Asked by CBS News whether there was more she could have done, Hyde-Smith said, "I think we worked very hard and had a very good campaign."
Hyde-Smith credited "a lot of money poured in" to the race for making it so competitive.
"We're just looking for the conclusion of our race and votes to be cast, votes to be counted," she added.
Burchett wants a GOP leader who will "admit" that Republicans "made mistakes"
Republican Rep. Tim Burchett of Tennessee told reporters he wants a House Republican leader who will admit Republicans "made mistakes."
"I want somebody that's going to message, and admit that we made some — we made mistakes," he said.
Burchett said Republicans failed to pass sufficient stock trading restrictions, and act on the cost of living. He said his party "let the oil companies make record profits."
A reporter asked Burchett if Republicans have learned their lessons from the midterms.
"We'd better or we'll continue to lose," he responded. "That's the bottom line. Congress, the Republican Congress deserves what it got because we allowed it to happen. But America doesn't deserve what they're getting ready to deserve."
Johnson says he will "take the oath in January"
House Speaker Mike Johnson said he will "take the oath in January" amid questions about his future in Congress.
"I'm going to take the oath in January and do everything I can to help my team succeed in the 120th Congress. We haven't thought much more beyond that," Johnson told reporters.
On Monday, Johnson declined to commit to serving out his full two-year term.
"We're focused on finishing the 119th [Congress] strong. We're going to do that. I'm still in charge here till early January, and we're going to do our duty. And after that, my commitment and my objective is to help my team ensure that the Republican Party has a very successful 120th Congress, and we'll see how all that develops, and that's my commitment," he said.
Johnson: Vote to table Hegseth impeachment "not going to fail"
House Speaker Mike Johnson said the vote that's planned for later Tuesday to sideline Massie's impeachment resolution against Hegseth is "not going to fail."
"We have the votes," he said. "We'll dispense with the impeachment gambit."
Scalise: "I've got a proven record"
After their candidate forum, House Majority Leader Steve Scalise said the difference between him and Rep. Jim Jordan is that "I've got a proven record."
"I could go to the most ruby red or the most swing district, and we're going to have to go back to those swing districts we lost," he said. "Also, great experience battling on policy, developing and shaping policy, because we're going to show an alternative agenda when the Democrats bring a socialist agenda to the floor."
House GOP is breaking for lunch
House Republicans are breaking for lunch and will return at 1:30 p.m. to elect their leadership team.
Why is Hegseth facing impeachment? The 8 articles on Iran, Maduro and more
Massie's impeachment resolution focuses on Hegseth's involvement in some of the most controversial episodes of President Trump's second term: the war with Iran, boat strikes in the Caribbean, an attack on an Iranian school and the capture of then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro.
The resolution includes eight articles:
- Article I: Waging war in contravention of the War Powers Resolution of 1973 Section 2(c)
- Article II: Waging war in contravention of the War Powers Resolution of 1973 Section 5(c)
- Article III: Waging war in contravention of the War Powers Resolution of 1973 Section 5(b)
- Article IV: Ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties
- Article V: Extrajudicial killings
- Article VI: Suppressing free speech
- Article VII: Kidnapping of a sovereign foreign leader
- Article VIII: Unlawful war in Yemen
GOP Rep. Nick LaLota on leadership pool: Scalise and Jordan are "two alphas in the room"
Asked whether there should have been a larger pool of candidates running for House GOP leadership given last week's electoral bloodbath, Rep. Nick LaLota of New York said, "It's pretty clear that those are the two alphas in the room who will lead us out of this minority."
Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan are facing off for the minority leader position.
Massie says he'll request separate votes on each impeachment article
In a post on X, Massie said that if his impeachment resolution advances, he will request a separate vote on each of the eight articles.
"I've heard from several members they agree with some of the Articles of Impeachment but not all of them," Massie wrote. "If the motion to kill my resolution by referring it to committee fails, and we proceed to the Articles themselves, I'll request a vote on each of the Articles separately."
GOP Rep. Nathaniel Moran: "We're having a very good family discussion"
Republican Rep. Nathaniel Moran of Texas said his party is having "a needed family discussion" during their candidate forum Tuesday morning.
"We're having a very good family discussion," he told reporters. "When you have a defeat like we saw last week, we certainly have to reevaluate where we are and how do we get back to the majority."
He added: "We all understand that coming out of today's leadership elections, whoever we select as our leaders … we have to be unified behind whoever we select."
Moran, who said he supports Majority Leader Steve Scalise for minority leader, said both Scalise and Rep. Jim Jordan "can speak very effectively and fervently" to the GOP base. But the party has "to speak to those swing districts and those swing voters that went to the Democratic side this time" to win back the majority in two years.
"We've got to have a voice that speaks to [the whole] spectrum of the Republican Party," he said.
Senate Republicans recess after 2-hour meeting
Senate Republicans recessed for committee hearings after meeting for around two hours Tuesday morning. They are expected to return at 2 p.m. to continue their discussion and vote on whether to delay leadership elections.
Sen. Ron Johnson, who has led the push to delay, told CBS News exiting the meeting that "it's a very high-quality conversation," and "people are voicing opinions on all sides of the issue."
Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky said around a dozen senators spoke during the meeting. Senators did not hear much from leadership yet, he said, adding that it "was mostly dissent."
Majority Whip John Barrasso said the meeting was a "very productive discussion."
Mike Johnson: GOP will "defeat" Hegseth impeachment push "one way or the other"
House Speaker Mike Johnson said Republicans will "defeat" Massie's impeachment resolution against Hegseth "one way or the other."
The House is expected to vote later Tuesday on a GOP motion that would effectively kill the resolution. It's unclear from Johnson's comments whether Republicans have enough support to table it, or if they would take another route to defeat it.
Johnson called Massie "a disgruntled congressman" and said the impeachment effort was "a political gambit for attention."
"This is just purely for people to get attention, and it's shameful," the Louisiana Republican said.
Rep. Don Bacon opposes Hegseth impeachment, says GOP leaders shouldn't be "rubber stamp" for Trump
Retiring Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska said he will oppose the effort to impeach Hegseth, after saying on Monday that he was unsure about how he would vote.
"I don't agree with the impeachment itself," Bacon said. "If you're allowed to amend it, I'd maybe feel a little differently."
He also said that House GOP leaders "can't just be a rubber stamp for the president."
"You got to stick up for what I would say are traditional conservative values," he said Tuesday morning. "And we did not do that this last two years."
Bacon also said he thinks it's time for new leaders to step forward, saying the House should be more of a "check and balance" on President Trump.
"I think the founders wanted us to be more of a check and balance. We should have pushed back on tariffs. We still should push back on tariffs. Tariffs cost us the election more than anything else, in my view," he said.
Rounds says most Senate Republicans "probably ready to vote"
Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota said "most of us are probably ready to vote, move forward," as Senate Republicans consider whether to delay their leadership elections.
"We can always have the discussions moving into the next year," he told reporters. "But I think today is a good time to get our leadership in place."
Rounds said, "There's nothing wrong or wrong with having a discussion about any changes that would be made in terms of what works."
Hawley rails against Senate GOP leadership
Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri expressed frustration heading into the Senate GOP leadership elections, telling CBS News he hoped to hear from leadership about "a different direction."
"This was the worst set of losses since Watergate, and Watergate was after one of the biggest political scandals in American history," Hawley said. "I mean, it's an incredible repudiation to the focus of this Congress over the last two years."
Hawley said he hadn't heard from Thune ahead of the leadership election.
"I, for one, haven't heard a word from the leader. So it can't be terribly important to vote today if the leader is not making calls and actually asking people to vote for him," he said.
Hegseth decries impeachment effort as "political spectacle"
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday defiantly denounced the impeachment effort led by GOP Rep. Thomas Massie, calling it a "farce" and "political spectacle" ahead of an expected vote in the House on the measure later in the day.
"What one disgruntled and defeated congressman is attempting is not oversight, and it's not accountability. It's a political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment," Hegseth said.
The defense secretary called Massie's impeachment effort an attempt to harm President Trump because of his own "personal animus" for the president and dislike of the Trump administration's policies.
"It's a farce, and it's a stunt, and everybody knows it," he said.
Thune says it's important Senate GOP "get some of these issues settled"
Thune was sympathetic on Monday to the efforts to come together on a path forward after the bruising midterm elections, and said that the decision over whether to delay the leadership elections would ultimately come down to his conference.
Thune said he was open to hearing the arguments for delaying the votes.
"But like I said, it's going to be a decision that's ultimately made by Republican senators," he said. "We'll hear them out."
"I think in the end, I think it's important that for purposes of moving forward, that we get some of these issues settled as soon as possible," Thune told CBS News Monday. "We'll see what our members think tomorrow."
Ron Johnson outlines push to delay Senate leadership elections
GOP Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, who's leading a push to delay the Republican leadership elections, outlined where things stood on Monday night, telling reporters that leadership had agreed to hold a conference meeting at 9 a.m. on Tuesday, "and we'll see how convincing those of us are who believe we should delay leadership elections."
When asked whether there needs to be new leadership, Johnson said Senate Republicans "just can't continue on business as usual" after a "stunning defeat" in the midterm elections.
"I mean, that kind of defeat demands change," he said.
Johnson conceded that there isn't a clear alternative to follow him as leader, saying, "That's part of our problem. Who'd want the job?" But he argued that at a minimum, Senate Republicans need to hear from their leadership team about the strategy moving forward.
"You need to have some real soul searching, some robust discussion, and give people a chance to consider, 'maybe I want to run for some leadership position,' and then give them a chance to talk to their colleagues to try and develop support," Johnson said. "You can't do that, you know, a week out of Washington, come back the next day. I mean, it's obnoxious."
Mike Johnson says Republicans can't delay House leadership elections, citing logistics
House Speaker Mike Johnson told reporters Monday night that Republicans can't delay their leadership elections because new members are in Washington for orientation and "it's just not something that logistically we could do."
"These dates were published in advance and everybody knew it. I suppose if you're running for an office, you'd always want more time to do that," Johnson said. "But the reason we can't change the date is because all this was set in stone, and we have all the new members here, and we're doing all the member orientation. If we delayed leadership elections, that interferes in all of that."
"There's a lot of logistics that goes into all that," he added.
Earlier Monday, GOP Rep. Jason Smith of Missouri, who chairs the Ways and Means Committee, argued that the elections should be delayed so that the conference could address rules that have allowed a small group of Republicans to hold up legislative activity throughout the past two years.
"Failing to address these issues before choosing someone new to lead our Conference is doing a disservice to whoever we choose as Republican Leader," he said. "We should delay our Leadership elections until we decide how to hold each other accountable and what our path forward should be. Our rules must never again permit a Leader to be taken hostage to the whims of an individual member."
Senate Republicans push for leadership election delay
Senate Republicans are scheduled to meet Tuesday morning as several GOP senators have pushed to delay their leadership elections.
Led by Sen. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin, a small group of Republicans signed onto a letter seeking to compel a conference meeting and vote on delaying the elections before moving forward. Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters on Monday that Republicans will "have a conversation" before seeing where the conference stands on holding the leadership elections.
"I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we'll see what the consensus of the conference is," Thune said. "I mean, ultimately, that's a decision that will be made by Republican senators sometime tomorrow."
Thune is expected to be reelected as leader, and no Senate Republicans have launched a challenge to his leadership. The South Dakota Republican said he was open to hearing the arguments for delaying the leadership election, adding, "I don't know if that solves anything." But he reiterated that the decision would come down to the GOP conference.
House Republicans face off for top spot after Mike Johnson bows out
House Republicans are set to meet at 9 a.m. to begin considering their next leadership team.
House GOP leadership could see the most significant change among the parties in both chambers after House Speaker Mike Johnson bowed out of leading the conference in the minority.
Johnson's move leaves Majority Leader Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, the House Judiciary Committee chairman, to jockey for minority leader.
"We have two extraordinary guys that are running to lead the conference. I'm close to both of them, and we'll see how that shakes out," Johnson said Monday.
Rep. August Pfluger of Texas is challenging Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota for the position of minority whip.
Republican Conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan has two opponents — Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida.
Mike Johnson doesn't commit to serving out another 2-year term
House Speaker Mike Johnson did not explicitly commit to serving out the full two-year term for which he won reelection last week.
"We're focused on finishing the 119th [Congress] strong. We're going to do that. I'm still in charge here till early January, and we're going to do our duty. And after that, my commitment and my objective is to help my team ensure that the Republican Party has a very successful 120th Congress, and we'll see how all that develops, and that's my commitment," the Louisiana Republican told reporters Monday night.

Senate GOP reelects Thune leader for next 2 years even after election losses

Senate GOP reelects Thune leader for next 2 years even after election losses
U.S. Senate Republican Leader John Thune, of South Dakota, speaks to reporters during a press conference in the Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Photo by Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom)
WASHINGTON — South Dakota Sen. John Thune will remain Republican leader next Congress despite the GOP’s loss of the chamber’s majority in this year’s midterm elections.
GOP senators voted behind closed doors Tuesday to keep Thune at the helm and reelected Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso as their whip. Neither was challenged.
The other members of Senate Republican leadership will include Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton of Arkansas, Republican Policy Committee Chair Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, Vice Chair of the Republican Conference James Lankford of Oklahoma and National Republican Senatorial Committee Chair Bernie Moreno of Ohio.
‘Listening intently’
Thune said after the meeting that he and other Republicans were not happy with the results of the midterm elections but will focus more on voters’ concerns in the years ahead.
“As we move forward, we are going to be listening intently to what the American people are saying,” he said. “And I think right now the issue that matters the most to them, like I said, is the cost of living.”
Thune pledged to extend the lame duck session that spans November and December to give Republicans more time to confirm nominees and approve legislation before handing over power to Democrats in early January. Republicans now hold 53 seats and The Associated Press projects they will have 44 next year, with results in Alaska and Mississippi still not called.
“Our conference is committed to being here to do whatever it takes to get as much done as we can,” he said. “That means extending the calendar here, the number of days we’re here, the number of hours we’re here, the number of votes we may end up taking. But we are going to finish this legislative session strong.”
Push for nominations
There was an attempt by several Republican senators to delay decisions about leadership for at least a week, but they were ultimately unsuccessful.
Missouri Sen. Eric Schmitt said after the meeting that Republican leaders had committed to clear as many nominees through the chamber as possible. Democrats are unlikely to approve President Donald Trump’s picks for the federal bench or administration roles after January.
“We’re definitely going to maximize the next 54 days for sure,” he said.
Missouri Sen. Josh Hawley said ahead of the vote that he wanted to delay until later this year to give Republicans an opportunity to “change course” following the election results.
“It’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here,” he said, questioning why Republican leaders didn’t put bills on the floor to lower the cost of gasoline and healthcare.
“If you don’t put people first, sooner or later people turn on you,” Hawley said. “And I think that this party thought we can just do whatever we want. People voted for us in ’24, we’ll do whatever we want. No you can’t. You’ve got to do stuff that actually helps people.”
‘Never disappoint voters again’
Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson said following a morning conference meeting that Republicans were “voicing opinions on all sides of the issues.”
“It’s one of those times in the Republican Conference, you kind of go, ‘We got … some smart people, and we’re having a very good respectful conversation,’” Johnson said.
Ohio’s Moreno said later in the day that Republicans are committed to “never disappoint voters again.”
“We’re firmly aware of the consequences now, and that’s the strategy we’re going to employ in 2028,” he said.
60 votes needed
Thune will still have considerable power as minority leader as long as Democrats keep a rule that requires 60 senators vote to advance legislation.
The hurdle forces bipartisanship on major proposals. But even if Democrats were to remove it next Congress, bills would still need Trump’s support to become law, unless there are supermajorities in each chamber to override a veto.

John Thune seeks another term as Senate Republican leader as the party reckons with election losses
Senate Republicans will be meeting for what they call a “robust conversation” on their future and to decide whether to keep South Dakota Sen. John Thune as their leader
WASHINGTON -- Senate Republicans will meet Tuesday for a “robust conversation” on their future and to decide whether to keep South Dakota Sen. John Thune as their leader, just a week after steep losses in the midterm elections that cost them their majority.
Thune is expected to be reelected, given that he remains popular with fellow Senate Republicans and is running unopposed. But some Republicans who returned to Washington on Monday for the first time since the election wipeout that cost them at least seven seats say it's too soon to endorse the status quo.
“We need to have some real soul-searching,” said Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson, who has circulated a letter to the conference asking for a delay in the closed-door, secret-ballot leadership elections. “We can't just continue on business as usual — that kind of defeat demands change.”
Still, Johnson conceded that there's no one else on the ballot.
“That's part of our problem, who would want the job?” he said, turning to a reporter and joking, “Do you want it?”
The angst comes as the party is just beginning to reckon with what the election results mean for GOP lawmakers and how soon they can try to rebuild their ranks. Two additional races remain uncalled in Alaska and Mississippi that could further deplete their numbers.
Thune made clear Monday that the leadership is moving ahead with Senate elections, which will include contests for other party leaders as well. But senators could still seek a vote to delay as they gather Tuesday morning.
Thune said they will have a “very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”
“Ultimately that’s a decision made by Republican senators,” Thune said.
Thune, who replaced Sen. Mitch McConnell of Kentucky as leader in early 2025, has spent much of the last two years navigating President Donald Trump, who has often been at odds with the Senate.
While backing up Trump on most policy, Thune has refused to change Senate rules and scrap the filibuster to pass voting legislation that would require proof of citizenship for all voters — a position that frustrated Trump and enraged some in the president's political base.
But Trump hosted Thune and his family at the White House in October. He said Monday that the GOP leader is “a very fine man.” The election is “up to the Senate,” Trump said.
Thune has made it a point to hear out different viewpoints before he makes major decisions and has maintained close relationships with the rank and file — a different approach from his predecessor, McConnell.
Thune “has widespread support” among Republican senators, said Oklahoma Sen. Jim Lankford, who said he supports having the elections on Tuesday when many of the new GOP senators are already in town for freshman orientation.
It is “a pretty complicated role to be able to manage,” Lankford said. “No one wants that job.”
Still, Johnson and others in his conference say Tuesday’s election is too soon.
Pennsylvania Sen. Dave McCormick in a statement over the weekend said Republicans shouldn’t choose a leader until the lessons of the election have been “digested and debated.” Indiana Sen. Jim Banks said Republicans need to “sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short.”
Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah, one of a few senators who signed Johnson's letter asking for a delay, said any leadership contest should come after the two outstanding Senate elections in Alaska and Mississippi are decided.
Neither of those races has yet been called, so it’s unclear if Republican Sens. Dan Sullivan of Alaska and Cindy Hyde-Smith of Mississippi will be returning to the Senate next year.
The soul-searching comes as lawmakers are trying to wrap up the year’s work — funding the government and seeing if there are some issues where they can work together, including an energy permitting bill that moved forward on a bipartisan vote Monday evening.
Republicans will try to confirm as many of Trump’s nominees as they can before the new Congress begins Jan. 3, and Democrats will strategize on how to best keep up their momentum into next year.
In his first remarks on the Senate floor since the election, which he called a “tough night," Thune previewed his pitch to his colleagues who are looking for answers on how they will navigate the minority.
Republicans will be willing to work with Democrats, Thune said, but “the American people are not looking for socialist government and leftist fantasies.”
Across the aisle, Democrats who could hold as many as 56 seats next year are having private discussions about whether New York Sen. Chuck Schumer is still the right person to lead them.
Schumer has found critics on the left and the right of his caucus as candidates from both sides declined to say in the campaign whether they would support him as leader. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen and Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin have both considered challenging Schumer, but neither has announced a run.
Many in the party have said it’s time for generational change after Schumer’s 12 years as leader. Still, Schumer appears to have widespread support from his members after carrying his party to massive wins in Tuesday’s elections.
Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, Schumer’s New York colleague and the head of the Democratic Senate campaign arm, predicted that he will win enough support. Schumer not only won the Senate back but he “cares deeply, and he understands politics well," she said.

sources.news_title: John Thune reelected as Senate GOP leader despite GOP losing majority
sources.text:
John Thune has secured reelection as the Senate Republican leader, navigating efforts to delay the vote despite the GOP losing its Senate majority in the recent midterm elections. This development comes as the Republican conference voted to proceed with the leadership election, overcoming attempts by several senators to postpone it. Thune, who became the GOP leader in early 2025 after Mitch McConnell, faced no competition for the position, ensuring continuity as Republicans transition to the minority. The final composition of the Senate remains partially unresolved, with key races in Alaska and Mississippi still pending.
Key Takeaways
- Thune’s reelection appears to indicate a unified Republican stance, potentially strengthening his candidacy for the Senate Majority Leader should the party regain control.
- Market pricing suggests increased confidence in Thune’s leadership role within the Republican party, although his path to majority leader depends on future Senate dynamics.
- The current 84% YES pricing for Chuck Schumer as the next Senate Majority Leader suggests markets are leaning towards a Democratic majority outcome.
What to Watch
The uncalled Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi are crucial for determining the final Senate composition, which will influence the majority leader outcome. Watch for any announcements from Republican senators, such as Steve Daines or Lindsey Graham, regarding potential leadership bids. Additionally, shifts in market pricing for Thune and other potential candidates could indicate changing expectations as the political landscape evolves.

WASHINGTON, DC — Senate Leadership Fund Executive Director Alex Latcham released the following statement in response to John Thune’s reelection as Senate Republican Leader:
“Senate Leadership Fund congratulates John Thune on his decisive reelection as Republican Leader. As a dedicated public servant and a steady conservative hand in the U.S. Senate, Leader Thune will continue to deliver on President Trump’s agenda as a principled fighter for the American people against Democrat obstruction and extremism. We thank Leader Thune’s colleagues for expressing strong confidence in his leadership as he guides Senate Republicans into the future.”

The House is scheduled to vote on the GOP motion later today to table Rep. Thomas Massie’s impeachment resolution against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Senate GOP leaders, facing pressure to delay their leadership elections, are meeting this morning to discuss the path forward after recent electoral losses.
House Speaker Mike Johnson stated that Republicans will “defeat” the impeachment resolution against Hegseth, while announcing a vote later today to effectively kill the measure. Retiring Rep.
